name: The Fate of Tlemcen
goal: Conquer the province of Tlemcen
outcome: Tlemcen made a fiefdom of Morocco
note: Morocco's war, begun two years before the campaign. Granada answered Morocco's call three days before it ended, and lost no one.

name: The Moroccan War on Castile
goal: Reclaim Andalusia
outcome: Defeat for Morocco: it gives up all its land on the Iberian side of the Strait (Trent's account).
note: Tunis and its vassals (Tripoli, Gabès, Gafsa, Touggourt, Bijaya) joined Morocco on 9 November 1338. Castile won the first five battles; Morocco took the sixth at Shalūqa in June 1339, and Tlemcen held al-Karash in August. Morocco's side holds Ishbīliyya and the whole Murcia area (Mursiyya, Siyāsa, Qarṭājanna, Lawraqa, Mūla); Trent's account has Tunisian troops taking Murcia. Granada can still be called in and has not been.

name: The War on Aragon
goal: Reclaim Andalusia (Granada's casus belli against Aragon)
outcome: Victory: Aragon cedes thirteen locations south of Castellón and Teruel, from Balansiyya and Shāṭiba to Uryūla and Jumalla, and pays war reparations for ten years
note: Declared on 24 May 1339 (confirmed by the save). Majorca, Navarre and Cagliari joined Aragon at once. Morocco and Tunis can be called in and have not been. The first fighting was a skirmish at Jumalla in August; on 8 November Ibn al-Khaṭīb won a great victory at Uryūla (Orihuela), worth 25 war score (Trent's screenshots), and laid siege to the town. Uryūla fell on 30 May 1340, as Castile laid siege to Mursiyya and cut the road home (Trent's account). Peace was made on 11 August 1340. Trent's account: with Aragon's field army down to some 6,000 against our 16,000, and our own supply in doubt, the sultan threatened to march on Barcelona; Aragon conceded everything south of Castellón de la Plana and Teruel, with a large indemnity.

name: The Second Moroccan War on Castile
goal: Reclaim Andalusia
note: Six years after its defeat of 1340, Morocco declares war again under the game's scripted Marinid casus belli to reclaim al-Andalus. Castile's alliances bring in Portugal and Aragon, with Majorca and Cagliari, so all three crowns of Iberia stand together. Tafilalt, Touat and Tlemcen march with Morocco at once; Tunis and its marches (Tripoli, Gabès, Gafsa, Bijaya and the Sahel) join on 18 October. Granada, Castile's tributary and alone on the Iberian shore, answered the call on 18 October and brought the Ṭāʾifa of Balansiyya with it; going to war with its overlord suspended the tributary bond. The Volunteers of the Faith rose again under Yaḥyā Raḥḥū (saves of 18 October and 8 November 1346; Trent's account). Tripoli, Gafsa and the Sahel had left Morocco's side by July 1348. Portugal made a separate peace on 2 September 1348, annulling its treaties with Castile for ten years and paying reparations (Trent's screenshot). On 27 January 1349 Castile, broken by the plague, made a separate peace with Granada alone, the Peace of Qurṭuba: Granada took 23 locations from Qurṭuba and Ishbīliyya to Jayyān, the Ṭāʾifa of Mursiyya took the Murcia area, Castile paid reparations and annulled its treaties with Aragon, and Granada returned to the name of Castile's tributary. Morocco fought on. Aragon made peace on 8 December 1350, giving Morocco the Balearic Islands and letting Tunis take Aragon's Sardinian vassal, the County of Cagliari, as its own subject; Majorca's lands on the mainland passed to Aragon on 1 January 1351. With Castile at the tipping point, Granada sold its promise not to fund the Marīnids for Qarmūna and the silver mines of Qusanṭīna, ceded on 21 May 1351. On 3 June Morocco surrendered to Castile, and the peace annulled Morocco's treaties with Granada (save of 3 June 1351; Trent's account).
outcome: Morocco surrenders to Castile (3 June 1351), keeping the Balearics but losing its alliance with Granada; Granada had already won the Peace of Qurṭuba (1349) and Qarmūna and Qusanṭīna (1351)

name: The Revolt of the Kingdom of Sevilla
goal: Independence for the Kingdom of Sevilla
note: The Castilian peasants of the lands won at the Peace of Qurṭuba and in 1351 rose and declared a Kingdom of Sevilla, taking all 25 of those locations (Qurṭuba, Ishbīliyya, Jayyān, Qarmūna, Qusanṭīna and the rest) in a war of independence. Qashtāla, Granada's overlord, joined on Granada's side, with the ṭāʾifas of Balansiyya and Mursiyya (save of 2 February 1353; Trent's account). The rebels raise few men (their manpower is about 360 against Granada's 3,100), but they hold the land. Granada crushed the rising before the Castilians could arrive: the rebels broke against the Granadan army at Sharīsh on 6 June, and their last army of 2,100 was destroyed at Shalūqa al-Kubrā on 27 June (save of 3 July 1353). The revolt ended on 5 July 1353: Qashtāla reaffirmed the old border, and all 25 locations returned to Granada (save of 5 July 1353).
outcome: The revolt is crushed: Granada destroys the rebel armies before Castile's arrive, and at the peace Castile reaffirms the border of the Peace of Qurṭuba; all 25 locations return to Granada (5 July 1353)

name: The Marīnid War for the Submission of Granada
goal: Morocco demands Granada's submission as its subject
note: Morocco declared war on Granada on 26 June 1360 under the Battle for the Strait's casus belli to demand Andalusī submission (the game calls it the First War for the Submission), with its subjects Tlemcen, Tafilalt and Touat. Granada is the target; Qashtāla joined as Granada's overlord and Portugal through its pact with Qashtāla. Qashtāla had only 87 men in its manpower pool after its war in Arghūn. The war allows up to 75% war score from battles. It came a year before Granada had meant to re-ally with Morocco for a war of independence, and despite relations of +150 (save of 26 June 1360; Trent's account). By June 1362 every attempt on Granada had failed: Granadan armies beat the landings at al-Mariyya (7 November 1360), Sharīsh (23 March 1361) and twice before Ishbīliyya (13 December 1361, 8 April 1362). Elsewhere the Marīnids ranged deep into Castile, breaking Castilian armies at El Escorial and Cáceres, and their and Tilimsān's fleets ruled the sea (save of 10 June 1362). About June 1362 Granada made a separate white peace with Morocco under threat of throwing its full weight into the war, with Morocco promising to respect Granada's territory; Castile and Portugal were left to fight on (Trent's account).
outcome: For Granada: a separate white peace on 30 July 1362, with Morocco's promise to respect its lands. For Castile: defeat. On 31 August 1365 Morocco took the north shore of the Strait, eleven towns from Ronda to Algeciras. In January 1366 it made nine of them into a fiefdom called the Kingdom of Sevilla (save of 5 April 1366).

name: The War of Independence
goal: Independence from Castile
note: On 20 May 1363, the day the truce with Castile ran out, Granada went to war for its independence and the amir marched north. The court had begun the claim on 31 December 1361; the casus belli the game gives is 'reclaim al-Andalus'. Castile came to it with only 183 men in its pool and 58 towns, Toledo among them, occupied by the Marīnids, with whom its war went on (Aragon now on Castile's side there). Portugal, which had made its own peace with Morocco, stood with Castile; the court's first aim was to knock it out of the war (save of 20 May 1363; Trent's account). The ṭāʾifas of Balansiyya and Mursiyya came to it untouched, having been kept out of the Marīnid war. Aragon joined Castile against Granada on 27 July 1363. Valencia and Murcia march with Granada; the Mamlūks could be called. On 1 August 1363 Yūsuf I died at Ayamonte on the march into Portugal; the war passed to his son Saʿd and the regent Naṣr al-Istijjī. Saʿd's army struck first into Portugal and laid siege to Lisbon, but the Portuguese army was not there. In the east Portugal and Aragon had joined forces and twice beaten the ṭāʾifas, at Cañete (1 March 1364) and Castellón de la Plana (5 April). The Granadan army marched east and chased them halfway across Iberia. It caught them at Zafra, Castilian land held by the Marīnids, and broke them on 3 August. It then destroyed what was left of the Portuguese and the Aragonese, one after the other, before Lisbon on 10 and 11 September (save of 11 September 1364; Trent's account). Portugal made a separate peace that same day, 11 September 1364. It gave up thirteen towns of the Algarve and the lower Alentejo, 83,000 people, which the court means to make a vassal state once the war is won. Castile and Aragon fight on. The ṭāʾifas held the line in the east: Valencia beat off an Aragonese squadron in the gulf of Valencia (25 September 1364) and a raid at Tortosa (9 March 1365), but the Murcian host was destroyed at Cuenca (27 June 1365) (autosave of 1 July 1365; Trent's account). Murād beat the Aragonese again at Cañete on 14 July 1365, and Aragon made its own peace on 2 September. On 6 January 1366 he destroyed the last Castilian army in the field, under the renegade Ibn al-Khaṭīb, at San Clemente. Castile made peace on 5 April 1366 (saves of 5 April 1366).
outcome: Victory. Granada declared its independence from Castile. Portugal (11 September 1364) gave up the Algarve and the lower Alentejo, thirteen towns. Aragon (2 September 1365) paid reparations. Castile (5 April 1366) gave up Niebla and Huelva, six towns. All three are to pay reparations for ten years. The game put Granada back under Castile as a tributary after the peace; Trent will remove that with the console.

name: The Mamlūk War on Cilicia
goal: Conquer a province of Cilicia (the Mamlūk sultan's casus belli from his council)
note: The Mamlūks, Granada's allies since 1349, went to war with Armenian Cilicia on 18 June 1364 with their subjects, and Granada and its ṭāʾifas were drawn in as allies. It is a war at the far end of the sea, fought in the middle of Granada's own (save of 11 September 1364).
outcome: Mamlūk victory. Twelve Cilician towns passed to the Mamlūks on 13 July 1365 (save of 5 April 1366, from the towns' change of owner).

name: The Second Marīnid War for the Submission of Granada
gameName: 1st War for the Submission of Granada
goal: Morocco demands Granada's submission as its subject
note: On 24 October 1368 Morocco declared war again under the Battle for the Strait's casus belli, which it had held again since 1 August 1367, to demand Andalusī submission. With it came its subjects Tlemcen, Tafilalt and Touat and its new fiefdom on the north shore, the Kingdom of Sevilla. In May Morocco had insulted Granada's envoys and broken the trade agreements. Granada fights with its three ṭāʾifas, and with the Mamlūks and their eleven vassals, allies again since January 1367. At the declaration Granada had 3,300 men under arms and 5 ships. Morocco had 800 men and 29 ships, Tafilalt 550 men, and the Mamlūks 3,000. Nobody had raised levies yet. The game counts this as the first war for the submission, although Morocco fought one in 1360 (save of 24 October 1368; Trent's account). Granada won the first battle at Cádiz on 11 November 1368. By March 1369 the Marīnid lands on this shore were subdued, all but the fortress of Cádiz, and the first Marīnid landing had been thrown back into the sea (Trent's account). By March 1369 the levies were up. Fās and its allies had 47,000 men under arms, 23,600 of them Moroccan, plus 77 ships. Granada's side had 113,000 and 59 ships, but 71,600 of those men were Egyptian. Granada itself had 8,800 and its ṭāʾifas 2,700. The war score stood at +31% for Granada (Trent's war screen). The war's first winter: Granada took Marbella, Gibraltar, Tarifa and the north shore, and Murād threw the first Marīnid landing back into the sea at Marbella (8 February 1369). Then Fās flooded men across the Strait. Jerez was lost and retaken. Osman relieved Cádiz and broke Khālid's assault on it (26 June). A landing at Málaga destroyed the Murcian host (16 September). The crown borrowed 469 from the estates to hire 4,800 mercenaries. Khālid held the line in the pitched battle at Antequera (15 October) and won at Almuñécar (8 November), and the first Mamlūk troops landed at Gérgal. By 18 November 1369 Morocco held the north shore again, except Niebla (save of 18 November 1369; Trent's account). After the November 1369 save, Khālid destroyed a landing at Adra (21 November) and held Málaga beside the first Mamlūk army (16 December), and again against Muṣliḥ al-Dīn (8 March 1370). The Mamlūks were thrown back at Jerez (31 March), and Khālid retook it six days later. A Marīnid landing in al-Gharb was destroyed at Beja (31 May). The last battle was fought at Málaga on 12 September 1370, the day of the peace (autosave of 1 July 1370; Trent's screenshots).
outcome: Victory. Morocco gave up the whole north shore of the Strait: Ronda, Marbella and the nine towns of its puppet Kingdom of Sevilla, which ceased to exist. It also paid reparations and signed an agreement against piracy. Granada's own losses came to about 13,000 men by the war screen at the peace, which counts attrition too. The 22 battles on record account for 9,900 of them, and for about 23,000 Moroccan dead. Granada's allies lost about 4,200 more.

name: The War of the Upper March
goal: The Reconquest of Iberia: Aragon's lands, at reduced cost (cb_reconquer_iberia, won with the Battle for the Strait)
note: On 1 December 1373 Granada declared war on Aragon under the Reconquest of Iberia claim, the second it had drawn up, six months after the truce of 1365 ran out. The sultan marched the armies of the realm to Balansiyya himself in early October and meant to fight with his regulars, raising levies only if he had to (Trent's account). Aragon fights with Sicily, the crown its king also wears, and Sicily's subjects Athens, Negroponte and a third; Sicily's allies Genoa, busy with its own war against Bologna and Pisa since May 1373, and the Pope did not join. The Mamlūks and their vassals came in on Granada's side, their galleys pointed at the shores of Sicily (Trent's account). At the declaration Granada had 3,300 men under arms, all regulars, and 4 ships; its ṭāʾifas none. Aragon had 400 men and 3 ships, Sicily 3 ships, the Mamlūks 4,050 men. Nobody had raised levies (save of 1 December 1373). The sultan's army of 3,300 met the Aragonese host of 5,300 before Barcelona on 29 January 1374. He gave the right wing and two-thirds of the cavalry to his brother Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī; the heavy infantry held the centre while the wings broke the Aragonese flanks, then closed on the levies in the middle. When it ended on 19 February, Aragon had lost 3,375 men and Granada 1,228, and the war score stood at +31% (Trent's account and battle screens). The sultan rode the remnant down at Tarragona on 9 March 1374: 1,343 of theirs killed or taken for 31 of ours, and the war score rose to +38%. All that was left of Aragon's army was 161 levies in the mountains (Trent's account). In late October 1374 the Mamlūk vassal of Barqa, under Shaykh Ramaḍān, took Malta, held for Sicily by its vassal Athens, with 2,900 men (Trent's account); on 12 November the Sicilian fleet sank all eight of Barqa's ships off the island. By January 1375 Granada had Barcelona under siege, and a second Mamlūk army of 4,272 under a Baḥrī cousin was marching through Girona to Castelló d'Empúries (6 January 1375, Trent's account). On 15 March 1375, with Barcelona 282 days under siege and Barqa's 3,000 ashore in Sicily after storming Siracusa, King Joan accepted peace: all of Aragon to Granada, Malta to the Mamlūks, reparations from Sicily, and the king's own safe passage to Palermo, alive and free. Montpellier had already gone over to England and Sassari to Arborea (Trent's account; saves of 15 March 1375). In battle Granada lost 1,260 men and Aragon 4,706.
outcome: Granadan victory. Aragon gave up every town it still held, 34 of them and half a million people, and ceased to hold land; Malta passed to the Mamlūks and Sicily paid reparations; King Joan was let go to Palermo (peace of 15 March 1375, war score +61%).

name: The War of the Aragonese Restoration
goal: The Reconquest of Iberia against Castile (cb_reconquer_iberia, the claim drawn up in March 1371); framed by the Emperor as the restoration of Aragon's lands, Saraqusṭa and the Aragonese heartland among them, to the renewed Kingdom of Aragon
note: On 5 June 1375, the day the truce of 1366 ran out, al-Andalus declared war on Castile under the Reconquest of Iberia claim. The Emperor framed it as the restoration of Aragon, whose heartland from Zaragoza to Teruel Castile held. The French were pushing the English into the sea, and if al-Andalus waited, Rome would rally France to blunt its advance; it could not afford to wait. A levy was laid on the nobles and on the ṭāʾifas, in gold and in men (Trent's account): the treasury stood at 1,579 against 286 in March. Rome and Lisbon answered the Castilian call: Portugal, in personal union with Castile since 1367, and the Papal States with three vassals, Faenza, Siena and a third. Egypt answered al-Andalus's, with its vassals; the four ṭāʾifas, Aragon and Catalonia among them, fought beside the Emperor (Trent's account; save of 5 June 1375). At the declaration al-Andalus had 3,300 men under arms, all regulars, and 4 ships; its ṭāʾifas 3 ships and no men. Castile had 1,750 men and 10 ships, Portugal 1,050 and 6, Rome 684 and 4, the Mamlūks 3,930. Nobody had raised levies. France, at +25% in its war with England, had 12,500 men in the field (save of 5 June 1375). The campaign opened in the east: on 12 December 1375 Alfonso de Oñate's 24,800 Castilians fell on the ḥājib Francesc's 6,100 Catalans at Chelva (Xelva) on the outskirts of Valencia, and the Catalans broke before the Emperor arrived. He gave battle there on unfavourable ground from 13 December, 13,800 against 23,900. The cavalry tried to sweep both flanks and the centre held by a thread, but on 14 January 1376 the field was lost: 8,169 of ours against 7,517 Castilians, and −12 war score (Trent's account and battle screens). A week later the Pope's 2,000, landed on the coast, destroyed the 2,567 Catalans left at Barcelona, and on 1 March the Portuguese and Castilian fleets sank or took 19 of Catalonia's 20 ships off Cape Ben Sakka (save of 13 January 1377). The alliance with Morocco was signed on 16 January 1376. By May 1376 the war score stood at −39%. Then the Pope landed an army on the Catalan coast, and on 25 May the Emperor destroyed it before Girona, 2,252 of theirs for 234 of ours (+3 war score; −36% after it). Defeat in detail, Trent wrote, will be the name of the game (Trent's account and battle screens). On 12 June Siena followed its master: its 1,558 men came against the Emperor before Girona and were destroyed to the last, for 101 of ours (+2 war score). With a Castilian army besieging Barcelona, the Emperor fell back on the old strategy of mercenaries and the faithful, raising more than 7,000 veterans from the Marches to relieve it (Trent's account, June 1376). Morocco, held out of the war by its truce with Castile, sent a gift of gold that paid for the mercenaries. On 16 August 1376 the second great battle was joined at Agramunt: 13,400 against 18,350, under the same Castilian general as at Šalba (Trent's account and screenshot). It ended on 1 September in slaughter: 12,724 of Castile's 19,073 lost against 2,839 of the Emperor's 15,038, +19 war score, and the war stood at −16% where it had been −42% two days before. The Mamlūk armies, though, were trapped across the sea by the far larger Iberian fleets. In early December 1376 the crown sent Catalan shipwrights to Alexandria, Damietta, Acre, Antioch and Tarsus to build shipbuilding wharves with Mamlūk coin and to teach the first modern galleys (Trent's account). On 31 January 1377 the Emperor broke the rebuilt Castilian army before Zaragoza, 5,675 of theirs for 705 of ours (+8), and on 13 June he crushed the last of it at Calatayud, 2,029 for 385 (+3); the war stood at +10%, and attention turned to the Portuguese (Trent's account and battle screens). On 30 September 1377, the day its truce with Castile ran out, Morocco answered the court's call and joined the war (Trent's account). In January 1378, with Valladolid under siege, the Emperor met the Portuguese at Sanlúcar la Mayor outside Seville and threw them back across the border, 8,343 of theirs for 1,069 of ours (+12); the war stood at +58% (Trent's account and battle screens). At sea, Morocco's fleet sank five Castilian ships off Cape São Vicente on 19 October 1377, though the Iberians sank Catalonia's last ship at Setúbal and three of Tlemcen's off Cape Mondego (save of 6 April 1378). By April 1378 Valladolid was weeks from falling, the Emperor's army was marching on Lisbon, the Moors had cleared a path through the sea and the first Mamlūk army was off the coast of Tunis. Offered peace or blood, as the Aragonese had been, the Iberians chose peace on 6 April 1378 (Trent's account; saves of 6 April 1378).
outcome: Victory for al-Andalus and the renewed Aragon. Castile restored the Aragonese heartland, 24 towns with Zaragoza, to the Ṭāʾifa of Aragon, gave up 46 towns of the Middle and Lower Marches with Toledo, Badajoz and Mérida to al-Andalus, and paid reparations (peace of 6 April 1378, war score +100%).

name: The Revolt of Ṭulayṭula
goal: Independence for a Kingdom of Toledo
note: On 1 December 1382 Toledo rose against al-Andalus, drove out its governor and damaged the madrasa in its heart (Trent's account). The revolt took 58 towns, about 520,000 people, nearly all Castilian and Catholic: the lands won from Castile in 1378, and also Murcia, Jaén, Úbeda, Baeza and the Huelva coast. The rebels raised 5,871 men, 5,420 of them levies, against the Emperor's 3,719 regulars; the ṭāʾifas joined the defence but had no men raised. Stability had fallen to 15. The Mamlūks and Morocco, as allies, were not drawn in (save of 8 December 1382). As in 1353, when the Kingdom of Sevilla rose, the rebels hold the land but cannot hold the field for long, Trent expects. The one great battle came at Montánchez (Munt Šāqir) on 22 February 1383, the rebels' 4,911 against the Emperor's 10,588; on 30 April he destroyed their last 1,807 men at Jaén for 44 of his own, and the rebellion ended that day (Trent's account and battle screens).
outcome: The revolt is crushed: the Toledan host is broken at Montánchez (22 February 1383) and its last army destroyed at Jaén on 30 April 1383, when the rebellion ends.

name: The War of the League
goal: The Reconquest of Iberia against Castile (cb_reconquer_iberia, ready from 1 January 1394)
note: On 4 March 1394 (1 Jumādā al-Ūlā 796) al-Andalus declared war on Castile for the third time, in the third war of the Istirdād. The court named it after the league Castile, Portugal and Andorra had sworn against the empire in 1393. It came a year after the truce of 1378 ran out. Castile had broken its union with Portugal in 1389, though the two stayed allied, and its king Fernando had died on 6 January; his son Pedro, twenty-three, faced the war. Castile, Portugal and Andorra had formed a coalition against al-Andalus in 1393. Portugal, the Papal States with Faenza and Siena, and Andorra joined Castile; the four ṭāʾifas, Morocco and its vassals, and the Mamlūks and theirs joined al-Andalus. At the declaration al-Andalus had 4,900 regulars and 16 ships; Castile 750 men and 19 ships, Portugal 1,550 and 7, Rome 1,750 and 14; Morocco 1,900 and 30 ships, the Mamlūks 4,050 (save of 4 March 1394; Trent's account). Castile's main host of some 24,000 fell first on the small ṭāʾifa armies around Sigüenza in August 1394. The Emperor's 17,650 chased it north through August and September, and on 12 October cut off its pursuit of an Aragonese army at Pamplona and beat it, 2,441 of theirs for 1,450 of ours (+5); Castile retreated in haste, and the war stood at +37% (Trent's account and screens). The Castilian host came back south in November, and on 5–14 December 1394 the Emperor caught it at Ejea de los Caballeros on unfavourable ground. Against Agustín Arce, Grand Master of Alcántara, he won anyway: 10,808 Castilians lost to 4,664 of ours (+20), and the war stood at +64% (Trent's account and battle screens). On 4 February 1395, 897 Aragonese riders caught the 10,886 survivors of Ejea at Peñafiel on the Duero and destroyed them, 10,564 lost without a single Aragonese casualty (+14). Portugal made its stand at Portalegre from 31 May 1395; on 18 June it broke, 7,087 lost to 3,744 of ours (+14), and the war score stood at +100% (Trent's account and battle screens). On 22 June 1395 (3 Ramaḍān 797) King Pedro surrendered at the Peace of Ramaḍān, and Portugal was made to follow (saves of 22 June 1395).
outcome: Victory. Castile gave up 51 towns, Madrid, Salamanca, Ávila, Cuenca and Cáceres among them, and paid reparations for ten years; Portugal gave up 20, Lisbon, Setúbal, Santarém and Évora among them (the Peace of Ramaḍān, 22 June 1395, war score +100%).

name: The Crusade of 806
goal: A crusade proclaimed by the Pope against al-Andalus, declared on the Ṭāʾifa of Aragon (cb_crusade)
note: On 1 February 1404 (19 Rajab 806) the Pope proclaimed the first crusade against al-Andalus and declared war on its subject, the Ṭāʾifa of Aragon; al-Andalus came in to defend it. With the Pope stood his vassals Faenza and Siena and a few princes of the Empire, Magdeburg, Cologne and Mainz among them: some 5,100 men under arms at the declaration, most of them levies, and 26 papal ships, the Pope's own regiments far under strength. With al-Andalus stood all six ṭāʾifas, the Mamlūks and their vassals (Mecca, Medina, the Dulkadirids, Barqa, Suakin and others) and Morocco with Tafilalt, Touat and Tlemcen. Al-Andalus had 4,900 regulars and 32 ships; the Mamlūks 4,050 men, Morocco 2,400 and 30 ships (save of 3 February 1404). The game ranked al-Andalus fourth among the powers. The papal fleet sank two Catalan ships in the first week, but the Moroccan and Catalan fleets swept it from the sea by August. On land the crusaders achieved nothing: Siena's contingent died at Aix in May. With French military access the Emperor marched on Avignon from 4 July and took the Pope's city. At Barjols in Provence the papal army beat off the Valencians on 10 October, and on the 20th the Emperor destroyed it. On 22 October 1404 (16 Rabīʿ al-Thānī 807) the Pope made peace.
outcome: Victory. The Pope was humiliated, paid 585 in gold and owes war reparations; no land changed hands (the Peace of Avignon, 22 October 1404).

name: The Risings of 807
gameName: 1st Rebellion Against Andalusia; 1st Rebellion Against Salamanca
goal: Three wars of independence against al-Andalus and the Ṭāʾifa of Shalamanka (cb_independence_war)
note: Ten weeks after the Peace of Avignon the conquered north rose. On 1 January 1405 (28 Jumādā al-Ākhira 807) the Portuguese lands proclaimed a Kingdom of Estremadura, 18 towns from Santarém and Torres Vedras to Évora and Elvas, and the Castilians of La Mancha and the Madrid country rose again as a Kingdom of Toledo, 30 towns from Madrid, Alcalá and El Escorial through Ciudad Real and Ocaña to Albacete, Hellín and Caravaca; Toledo itself, Lisbon and Setúbal stayed loyal. On 2 January the Leonese of the Ṭāʾifa of Shalamanka rose as Ciudad Rodrigo, taking 16 of its 21 towns, Salamanca, Ávila and Plasencia among them. Al-Andalus held 100 towns of its 148, and 1,295,000 of its 1,841,000 people. The rebels had some 11,000 men, nearly all levies: Toledo 5,100, Ciudad Rodrigo 3,100, Estremadura 2,900; al-Andalus 3,400 regulars and the ṭāʾifas 1,250 (save of 7 January 1405). Estremadura laid siege to al-Ushbūna. The game gives rebellion battles no war score. The war's battles were Buitrago (28 January, Toledo over Qūnka's few men), Cuenca (18 March, the new Emperor's first battle), Granadilla (2 July, Khālid ibn Yaḥyā's joint host over Ciudad Rodrigo), Cuenca II (10 July) and al-Ushbūna (5 August, where al-Gharb threw back Estremadura) (saves of 8 July and 24 August 1405).
outcome: Victory. Ciudad Rodrigo fell apart on 8 July 1405, six days after Granadilla, and its sixteen towns went back to the Ṭāʾifa of Shalamanka. The Kingdom of Toledo and Estremadura collapsed on 24 August 1405, and their forty-eight towns returned to the crown.

name: The War of Jillīqiya
goal: The Reconquest of Iberia against Castile (cb_reconquer_iberia), declared the day the truce of the Peace of Ramaḍān ran out
note: On 29 June 1410 (25 Ṣafar 813) the truce of 1395 ran out and the Emperor Ismāʿīl declared war on Castile at once. Portugal joined Castile. Fās answered the Emperor's call with Tlemcen and Tafilalt; the Mamlūks were busy in the Fertile Crescent and not needed (Trent). On the day of the declaration al-Andalus had 4,900 regulars and 53 ships, Morocco 2,400 men and 37 ships; Castile 1,650 regulars and 25 ships, Portugal 750 and 8. No levies had yet been raised (save of 29 June 1410). Castile capitulated on 2 September 1411. Portugal fought on, and the Emperor refused a separate peace for concessions: this war was to be the end of Portugal (Trent, September 1411). The Emperor Ismāʿīl named it the War of Jillīqiya, the old Arab name for the whole Christian north-west beyond the Duero, the country the armies of al-Manṣūr had marched through to Shant Yāqub; it is the fourth war of the Istirdād.
outcome: Victory. Portugal was annexed whole, 34 towns, and Castile gave up 63, Old Castile, León and Navarre, keeping 45 in the north with its capital at Oviedo (the Peace of Rajab, 1 November 1411).

name: The Rising of Zamora
gameName: Independence war of Zamora against the Ṭāʾifa of Liyūn
goal: A war of independence against the Ṭāʾifa of Liyūn (cb_independence_war)
note: On 1 June 1420 (19 Jumādā al-Ūlā 823) the Castilians of the province of Zamora, in the Ṭāʾifa of Liyūn, rose under Eduardo de Avellaneda. Al-Andalus and all its ṭāʾifas were bound to Liyūn's defence; Valencia left the war on 1 August, the day it was taken into the crown. The rebels never had more than a few hundred men under arms. The war's one battle was Fermoselle (10 August), where the Emperor Ismāʿīl destroyed them (save of 11 August 1420).
outcome: Victory. The rising was over on 11 August 1420, the day after Fermoselle. Liyūn lost no towns.

name: The Mamlūk War on the Ottomans
goal: An attack on the Ottomans before they could attack Egypt (the Mamlūk casus belli 'attack threat')
note: The Mamlūks of Miṣr, allies of al-Andalus since 1367, declared war on the Ottomans and Nafusa, in the mountains of Tripolitania, on 19 September 1423 (13 Shawwāl 826), and on 1 October (25 Shawwāl 826) called the Emperor to arms. Joining cost al-Andalus 20 trust with the Ottomans; there was no truce to break. The Emperor answered the call, and the court hoped the Mamlūks did not expect much of it (Trent's account and screenshot of 1 October 1423). The Ottoman sultan Aḥmad is the brother of the Emperor's wife ʿĀʾisha. Al-Andalus and all seven of its ṭāʾifas came in that day. It was over in under eleven months: Nafusa made peace on 23 July 1424 and the Ottomans on 8 August (save of 14 August 1424).
outcome: Mamlūk victory. Thirty-seven towns of central Anatolia, from Kayseri and Niğde to Malatya and Çorum, passed to the Mamlūks on 8 August 1424. Al-Andalus took nothing; its truce with the Ottomans runs to 8 February 1436 (save of 14 August 1424).

name: The War of Shant Yāqub
goal: The Reconquest of Iberia against Galicia (cb_reconquer_iberia), the greatest of the successor states of Castile
note: Muḥammad V wanted his father's work finished at once and ordered the army north against Castile. His sons, the princes Ismāʿīl and Aḥmad, talked him round: Galicia would be the nobler and harder conquest, and Navarre the next, since the Basques were a far more redoubtable people than the Castilians. On 18 May 1430 (24 Shaʿbān 833) war was declared on Galicia (Trent's account). All seven ṭāʾifas came in with the crown; the Mamlūks, Fās and Tūnis were called but had not yet answered. Galicia stood alone, with 31 towns, two ships and no army in the field, against al-Andalus's 4,600 regulars and fifty ships; Castile, allied to the Angevin Empire and Navarre, was not involved (save of 18 May 1430). The war is named for Shant Yāqub, Santiago de Compostela, Galicia's capital, which al-Manṣūr took in 997. On 5 August 1430 the last Galician army, 3,229 men, threw itself on the army of the Ṭāʾifa of Liyūn, 5,602 under Juan Cangas, at Oviedo and was destroyed to the last man (save of 17 August 1430).
outcome: Galicia annexed whole at 82 war score at the Peace of Ṣafar (3 November 1430, 16 Ṣafar 834): its 31 towns, from Santiago and A Coruña to Oviedo and Llanes, came to the crown. The same day the eight towns of old Asturias went on to the Ṭāʾifa of Liyūn and the other 23 were made the Ṭāʾifa of Jillīqiya under Diego Sotomaior. King Diego Villamarín went into exile at Augsburg (saves of 3 and 5 November 1430).

name: The War of the Mountains
goal: The Reconquest of Iberia against Navarre (cb_reconquer_iberia), and with it Castile, Navarre's ally
note: With Galicia beaten but the peace not yet made, the two princes saw an opening. Navarre had allied itself to Castile, and while Castile was under the protection of London, Navarre was not. The war would have to be swift, but most of the empire's armies were already in the north: if they overwhelmed both before the Angevins decided whether they were bound to help, the crown had its chance. On 17 August 1430 (27 Dhū al-Qaʿda 833) war was declared on Navarre, and Castile alone answered its call (Trent's account). In the declaration save Navarre (10 towns, 7 ships) and Castile (4 towns, 2 ships) had no men under arms; the Angevin Empire, Castile's ally, was not in the war. Named for the last kings of the mountains, the Cantabrian and Basque north where Qashtāla had begun. On 3 November 1430 the army of al-Andalus broke 3,580 Navarrese before Bilbao, and all three kingdoms fell (Trent's account; save of 3 November 1430).
outcome: Navarre and Castile annexed at 59 war score at the Peace of Ṣafar, the same day as Galicia (3 November 1430, 16 Ṣafar 834). Navarre's ten Basque towns, from Bilbao and San Sebastián to Vitoria, went on to the Ṭāʾifa of Banbalūna; Castile's last four, Santander, Laredo, Potes and San Vicente de la Barquera, to the Ṭāʾifa of Burghush. The Kingdom of Castile ceased to exist, and the Angevin Empire never entered the war. It was the last war of the Istirdād: Iberia was conquered, and Book V closed (saves of 3 and 5 November 1430; Trent's account).

name: The Crusade of 835
goal: A crusade proclaimed by the Pope against al-Andalus, declared on the Ṭāʾifa of Aragon (cb_crusade) and aimed at the province of Barbastro

attackers: Genoa's subjects Orange, Arborea, Corsica, Cuneo and Gazaria

note: Fifteen months after the Emperor Muḥammad had the cathedral of Santiago pulled down, on 1 October 1431 (23 Muḥarram 835) the Pope, Fabrizio Ricci, proclaimed the second crusade against al-Andalus and, as in 1404, declared war on its subject the Ṭāʾifa of Aragon, whose king Rodrigo de Borja is the brother of the Emperor's wife Magdalena. The Emperor answered for him, and every ally came in the same day: the eight ṭāʾifas, the Mamlūks with Mecca, Medina, Barqa, Suakin and their other vassals, Morocco with Touat and Tlemcen, and Tunis with Tripoli, Gabès, Touggourt and Gallura. The Church's call brought the Pope Provence, Ireland and its lordships, Iceland, the archbishops of Cologne and Trier and a scatter of German princes; the Pope himself held three towns, no army and thirteen ships. The Angevin Empire stayed out. On 3 October Genoa, Siena and Aquileia joined, Genoa with Orange, Arborea, Corsica, Cuneo and Gazaria, and the Genoese fleet of 24 ships became the crusade's strength at sea (Trent's account; saves of 1 October and 1 December 1431). In the first two months the Tunisians were thrown back at Oristano in Sardinia (20 November) and lost a ship to the papal squadron in the Gulf of Talamone (26 November). In May 1432 the Emperor ordered a series of shipyards built to give al-Andalus a navy to counter Genoa's (Trent). Through the winter the war was fought in the Tyrrhenian Sea, in Lazio and in Sardinia, and al-Andalus's own army did not fight. The papal admiral Vukmir Janković destroyed a Tripolitan squadron of fourteen in the Gulf of Talamone (5 December) and, with fifteen Genoese ships, sank or took fifteen of twenty-four Tunisian ships off Lazio (20 December). Then the Moroccan and Tunisian fleets came up together: nine papal ships were lost in the Gulf of Olbia (27 January 1432), seventeen of Aquileia's twenty-eight in the Gulf of Orosei against 185 Muslim sail (1 February), and Vukmir's last five in the Corsica Channel (14 March). On land the Tunisians landed in Lazio and Sardinia with mixed fortune. The crusaders' army in Tuscany, led by an Andalusī Muslim mercenary, Khayr al-Dīn Khayyām, beat them at Tivoli (31 December) but was broken by the Moroccans at Pitigliano (26 March). In the Atlantic, Mecklenburg's and Ireland's fleets beat small Portuguese and Burgalese squadrons off Ushant and Saint-Malo. On 1 May 1432 the war score stood at 4 in the allies' favour, and seven Andalusī arsenals and seven war galleys were under construction (save of 1 May 1432). In the spring the last Tunisians in Lazio were destroyed at Terracina (17 May) and the Moroccans were beaten off at Viterbo (1 June). Off Cape Mondego on 27 June the Mecklenburg fleet attacked 32 Catalan ships and 8 of the crown under Berenguer Ramon of Catalonia and lost 18 without sinking one, the first fight of the Emperor's own ships in the war. Friuli and Lower Carinthia joined the crusade in July.
outcome: A peace of the Pope's asking, 27 July 1432 (28 Dhū al-Qaʿda 835), at war score 5. At war with Mantua and Milan on another front, the Pope paid al-Andalus 114.64 gold at once and a tenth of his income for five years in reparations (36.45 gold a month at the peace), and annulled all his treaties with Genoa, Siena and Aquileia. No land changed hands (Trent's account and screenshot; save of 27 July 1432).
